items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Abstract The three companions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] use three structures side by side: probability laws and kernels, provenance (which source a record came from), and differentiation at the boundary of the simplex. This paper studies how they fit together, one layer at a time. Every ingredient of Step 1 is standard in categorical probability; what this step contributes is a set of exact statements about where the ingredients fail to commute, which the later steps build on. The finite distribution monad Dand the provenance comonad W= L×(−) are related by a distributive law λ: WD⇒DW, (l,p) →δ l ⊗p. All four axioms are written out with their types and proved. Its two-sided Kleisli category is the category of Markov kernels indexed by a source, with one source held throughout a composite. Marginalisation is total and affine. Event conditioning is partial and nonlinear. It is undefined exactly where the event has probability zero, it cannot be extended continuously to that wall, and its derivative grows like 1/p(A) near it. Conditioning commutes with marginalisation only for events that are cylinders over the kept coordinates. Contextual Bayes decomposition. Conditioning a pooled law equals pooling the conditioned sources with Bayes-updated weights. In the worked example, source weights 1 3 4 , 4 become 8 15 23 , 23 , and keeping the old weights gives the wrong answer ( 63 160 instead of 9 23 ). Forgetting provenance is marginalisation over the sources. It commutes with every window, but it is not injective: two families of sources can share a pooled law and every pooled table while differing in every labelled table. Step 2, the tangent layer. The cone tangent structure of the tangent companion commutes with the provenance comonad. Each source is a face of the labelled simplex, and a feasible direction leaves that face exactly when it injects whole records under another label; after forgetting provenance, an injected source and a drifting source have the same direction. Marginalisation and conditioning map feasible cones onto feasible cones, with explicit lifts; conditioning’s lift shrinks like p(A) near its wall. The cone T k Hof the half-line is generated by elementary tensors, so it is closed under products, and pooling is a morphism at every order: the pooling paradox lives in the decision functional, not in pooling. Differentiating the contextual Bayes decomposition splits every sensitivity into a reweighting term and a within-source term; in the worked example the answer 9 16 23 moves at rate− 529 per unit of small-trial share. Strata and jumps. The sources that survive conditioning are exactly those with π l p l (A) > 0. Conditioning maps fibres of forgetting onto fibres: it keeps provenance ambiguity on the event, discards it off the event, and can destroy identifiability but never create it. Inside 1 its domain, conditioning moves at rate at most 2/P(A), so nothing jumps and a sudden change needs a rare event. At the wall the limit is the conditional of the path’s leading jet; analytic passages are removable, and jumps need a kink, a non-analytic path, or a jump of the law. Step 3, orders of transitions. On non-negative germs in a Hardy field, order is a semiring homomorphism to (min,+), so every layer operation has an exact order calculus. Each source reaches an event at its own order. The sources of least order survive conditioning, with weights given by leading coefficients; the others vanish at their extinction orders. The two sides of a transition carry independent order data, analytic passages are removable but smooth ones need not be, and flat approaches have limits inside a Hardy field but not outside. items.summary: The magnetotelluric (MT) method uses natural electromagnetic field variations to image subsurface electrical resistivity at depths ranging from tens of metres to hundreds of kilometres. It is widely used in geophysical exploration for natural resources, including minerals, geothermal energy, and groundwater, as well as in the characterisation of sites for CO$_2$ storage and in studies of crustal and lithospheric structure. The MT inverse problem is, however, inherently non-unique: many distinct resistivity models reproduce the observations equally well. Conventional practice nonetheless reports a single regularised model, with no quantitative measure of its uncertainty. MTGeophysics.jl is a Julia package developed to address this limitation. Its principal aim is the quantification of uncertainty in MT model building, advancing interpretation from a single deterministic model, through an ensemble of plausible models, towards the full posterior distribution. The package also provides tools for data analysis, mesh generation, masking, forward modelling, inversion, model analysis and visualisation for MT research and applications. MTGeophysics.jl v0.7.3 No breaking changes. Polishing docs for JOSS

items.summary: The calibration and test probabilities of every run of a tabular classification benchmark, released so that prediction sets and their metrics can be recomputed without refitting a model. A conformal set is a function of four arrays: the class probabilities and labels on a calibration split, and the same on a test split. This deposit is those arrays, together with the software that reads them. The benchmark comprises 218 classification datasets and 22 models from four families, among them 13 tabular foundation models, each evaluated with the same ten seeds. Of the 218, 178 are real datasets and 40 are a synthetic block generated for this benchmark; three of the real ones are Bayesian-network resamplings of small classical datasets and are much larger than their seeds; of those, only one has its own seed in the collection, so that pair is not independent of itself while a rank test treats datasets as independent. Dataset size does not indicate provenance: the largest datasets in the collection are real. Coverage is not uniform and the per-model dataset count is reported for every cell. Eleven datasets carry more than ten classes, and the in-context models measured on them cannot enter them: one refuses and names the limit, another builds a ten-output head and fails inside a kernel. That is a capability limit observed on the models that were run rather than a property claimed of the family, and it is not missing work. One foundation model is measured on the original datasets only. Anything computed across models should be computed on a complete submatrix: the datasets on which every model being compared has all ten seeds. The calibration rows are held out of fitting, of tuning, of early stopping and of the in-context data, and each cell records which rows they were. The code that does it is included, with the line of each step documented. Probabilities are float64 and are not rounded: a prediction set is a comparison against a threshold, and a point sitting on that threshold moves if the value it is compared to is shortened. The data are released under CC BY 4.0. The software included in the source archive is released under the MIT licence, as stated by the LICENSE file it contains. The datasets themselves are not redistributed: each cell carries the row indices into its source dataset, and the synthetic datasets regenerate from their seeds with an included script. Model weights are not redistributed; every checkpoint is named in the model table. Version 1.2.0 adds the runs completed after version 1.1.0 and changes or removes nothing in it. Three new shards (cells-011 to cells-013, 2.02 GB) hold 311 further cells; index.parquet now lists all 46,182 cells and manifest_1016.parquet is their manifest. The files prefixed blocks_1016__ recompute the two blocks outside the main comparison on the completed runs, with the pipeline that produced the article's tables: the large-dataset block on 49 datasets and 21 models (42 in version 1.1.0) and the many-class block on 11 datasets and 7 models (5 in version 1.1.0). The main block of 113 real datasets and 22 models is unchanged. CHANGELOG.md lists what is added and the pairs that are still missing, with the reason for each.

items.summary: This Version 2.1 report places the Maxwell Mass Effect at the forefront of a coherent model for the Venusian atmosphere. The surface temperature is treated as the dependent variable required to support the atmospheric mass against gravity. Solar energy is captured in a shallow topside thermal heating pool, stored as potential energy, and returned to depth by organised descent in the polar vortices under conservation of angular momentum. The sulfuric-acid lifting condensation level (LCL) acts as the thermodynamic anchor (Dew-Point Anchor Hypothesis). A two-component radiative opacity lapse rate then fixes only the geometric separation between that LCL and the infrared emission level. Stochastic inverse modelling with a VIRA equatorial profile, hydrostatic integration and thermodynamic filters recovers a cloud base near 49.6 km, an emission level near 69.4 km at approximately 229 K, and a surface pressure of approximately 91.5 bar. An order-of-magnitude energy-budget test shows that the required polar mass flux lies within the range of observed vortex descent speeds. Version 2 adds a quantitative recirculation (recycle) test using existing Venusian meridional circulation wind data. Observed poleward flows of ~10–15 m s⁻¹ at cloud tops imply a hemispheric Hadley-cell mass flux of order 10¹¹ kg s⁻¹ and a full recirculation timescale of 1–2 weeks. This multi-cycle pathway resolves the apparent single-pass temperature-rise tension and brings the adiabatic signature into agreement with observed polar temperature contrasts of 15–50 K. The same boundary conditions can be satisfied by a conventional greenhouse calculation, but only the Maxwell framework supplies a structural explanation for the polar vortices themselves and a dynamically consistent energy pathway. A new Discussion section explains the changes from Version 1 and how they address independent criticisms of the energy-budget magnitude and the need for a discriminating quantitative test. Diagnostic figures from the inverse model and the recirculation test are included.

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse break-point analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. items.summary: Phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) is the practical method for large arrays of optical traps, but it optimizes the hologram on an ideal model of the spatial light modulator (SLM), and the sequences that move traps interpolate between holograms that were never optimized for the frames in between. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. On a 10 x 10 lattice behind a crosstalk device, the relative standard deviation falls from a median of 5.21 percent for phase-fixed WGS at 30 iterations (5.21 percent at 100) to 0.205 percent, a median factor of 26 over 5 seeds (range 16 to 33) at a median 0.995 of the baseline's efficiency; the factor is 7.9 with 4-bit phase and a fill factor of 0.85 added, and 2.0 on a smaller 8 x 8 grid with flicker added and a fixed 30-iteration budget (the ratio of the means of 3 seeds); over the 5 geometries of the studio's benchmark on that device the median factor is 1.73 (0.97 to 4.69), and 2 of them meet both thresholds. A control that removes the device model from the loop gains nothing (5.14 percent), so the gain comes from the model. Second, optimizing every intermediate hologram of a moving-trap sequence with the trap phases locked to a smooth trajectory (flicker-bounded sequence) keeps the minimum transient intensity of the moving traps at a median 0.920 of their mean (range 0.915 to 0.932) over 5 seeds at 13 frames (below 0.9 at seven frames), against 0.654 (0.551 to 0.709) for linear phase interpolation. On longer moves, with the frames that keep the peak step per frame at most 0.2 Fourier units, the bound is met on 6 and 6 of 8 seeds of two lattice moves and on 5 of 6 seeds of a rearrangement case; the seeds that miss it miss it on the phase path their end phases prescribe, and at an equal number of frames on the rearrangement linear phase interpolation leads. Both results hold in a model of a simulated device and in a transient model that we define; neither is a hardware measurement. Description: A Hybrid, Category-Theoretic Framework for Artificial General Intelligence: Architecture for Continuous Learning, Causal Reasoning, and Self-Improvement Author:  Luigi Usai Abstract: Current advancements in artificial intelligence, particularly Large Language Models, demonstrate impressive generative capabilities but often lack robust mechanisms for persistent knowledge integration, causal reasoning, and autonomous, goal-directed behavior. This paper presents a novel, hybrid architecture for Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) that addresses these limitations by integrating symbolic reasoning, sub-symbolic pattern recognition, and a sophisticated cognitive control loop. The system's core is a probabilistic Knowledge Base (KB) built on RDF, where each fact is associated with a confidence score that evolves over time. A key contribution of this framework is its use of Applied Category Theory as a primary learning mechanism; perceptions are structured into a "Category of Perceptions," and learned concepts form a "Category of Concepts," with functors mapping between them to represent abstract patterns. Higher-order cognition is achieved through the analysis of natural transformations between these functors, enabling meta-learning and analogical reasoning. The AGI's autonomy is driven by an intrinsic motivational system based on cognitive drives such as curiosity and knowledge coherence, which guide a symbolic planner. To ensure robust world models, the system employs an Active Causal Inference module that identifies weak causal links in its KB, designs, and executes experiments to test them. Furthermore, the architecture features a powerful self-improvement mechanism, capable of analyzing its own source code, generating optimized versions via an integrated LLM (DeepSeek), and validating them through an automated testing framework. A case study in the domain of chess demonstrates the system's ability to develop and utilize a novel, non-textual chromatic language (ColorZip) for visual reasoning and strategic analysis.
